title: Native sample scope and preparation
lead: The native apps provide source and playback editors, applied configuration code, source switching, and live rewind controls. Platform-specific settings include Apple video scaling and initial track preferences, Android language and retry settings, and external WebVTT subtitles. The Web app provides the broader configuration panel; use each platform chapter for build steps, defaults and verified playback scope.

blocks.text: The source catalogs include external public reference streams. The configuration forms also accept your own reachable test URLs. Available formats, audio, subtitles, and live rewind windows depend on the source and platform. Native apps do not automatically load the media bundled with Pages.

items: Start with a VOD preset to compare settings without a moving live window. Confirm that video plays before editing. Use a source with the audio tracks, subtitles or bitrate variants required for the feature you want to try.

Open the configuration editor and Show applied code. Keep the current values as a baseline, then edit the setting you want to compare. Draft text does not change the running player or its exported code.

Read the action before Apply. Source-only changes reload the existing player on Apple and Android. Player changes recreate it. React Native and Vega recreate it for any changed configuration. The platform chapters give example values and units.

Apply, wait for the new source load, and check the actual picture, playback controls and event log. Reopen Show applied code to confirm the submitted values. A value in code confirms the configuration; it does not by itself prove that a stream contains a matching track or bitrate.

To discard unapplied edits, use the platform's Reset control. To undo an applied experiment, re-enter the baseline values and Apply again. Reset does not undo a completed Apply. The Android player Reset prepares SDK defaults instead of restoring the applied player values.

blocks.text: The editors expose selected SourceConfig, PlayerConfig and platform-specific settings, together with application preferences. The Web app provides broader lists, including TweaksConfig. Editable examples include:

items: Source: HTTP/HTTPS URL and type, optional title and poster URL, start offset in seconds, and offset reference.
Player: autoplay, startup mute, forward buffer in seconds, and bitrate cap in bits per second. Supported formats, blank/default meanings, and numeric limits differ by platform.

Apple: native video scaling through StyleConfig.scalingMode, plus initial audio/subtitle language preferences implemented by the app with public track-selection APIs. See the Apple chapter for application at the first Ready event and native HLS subtitle requirements.

Android: player-wide and source-specific audio language priorities, external WebVTT track metadata, and HTTP retry delays. See the Android chapter for inheritance, subtitle-menu selection and retry units.

React Native and Vega: an external WebVTT URL, label and language. React Native exposes default-track metadata; Vega can enable the track on load. See the native integrations chapter for the different display and selection paths.

blocks.text: Invalid input leaves the applied configuration unchanged. Reset changes only the draft: Apple, React Native, and Vega restore applied values; Android restores the applied source or SDK player defaults, depending on the Reset button. Android accepts a valid Apply again even with the same values, repeating the source reload or player restart. Applying unchanged settings does nothing on Apple, React Native, and Vega.

Apple shows current native track selections and provides initial track preferences. Android audio priorities influence startup selection. Default-track metadata on Android and React Native does not itself enable subtitles; use their player subtitle menus. Vega displays enabled external WebVTT cues as plain text. Other track and quality controls depend on the SDK UI, source and platform.

blocks.text: Native playback requires your own Player license and permission for the application identifier. The Web SDK’s localhost exception does not apply. If you use Analytics, allow the application identifier on that license as well. Update the permissions if you change an identifier. Normal native playback does not require an account API key.

blocks.text: Run the common preparation from the repository root using Node.js 24.19.0 and pnpm 10.33.0. Create the root .env file from .env.example and enter your own licenses. The Analytics license is optional; leaving it empty disables the collector. The following example contains a placeholder.

blocks.title: Run from the repository root
blocks.text:
pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
bash scripts/sync-env.sh
pnpm --filter @showcase/ui-shared build
pnpm sync:webui

sync-env.sh writes ignored Apple, Android and React Native license files. Follow the platform chapters to generate and build the native app. The native integrations chapter covers the included Expo generator and Kepler host; Vega additionally requires its separately installed SDK and runtime:config, which sync-env.sh does not run. After a license change, repeat the relevant configuration step and rebuild. Keep generated configuration files, license values and local SDK paths out of the public repository.

DVR is the available rewind window in a live stream. These samples use 0 for the live edge and negative values for the past. −30s seeks to 30 seconds behind the live edge; it does not rewind 30 seconds from the current position. The requested position is clamped to the range reported by the SDK.

blocks.text: HLS may report a rewind window of 0 seconds just after startup. Start playback and wait for the range to become available. Increasing the forward buffer does not extend the historical media retained by the stream. The live edge keeps moving while a seek completes. Acceptance of a seek request, completion inside the SDK, and the UI update do not happen at the same instant.

blocks.title: What Allow DVR controls
blocks.text: This switch controls the sample’s state calculation and helper rewind buttons. It does not change a global SDK DVR setting or guarantee that all seeking, including the shared UI’s seek bar, is disabled. Toggling it also does not move playback to the live edge. Use Live edge or Go to live edge to return to live. Apple and Android expose a separate SDK live time-shifting setting in the player editor; Allow DVR does not edit that setting.
